summary:
Kayseri stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward LGBT people has been formalised as state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring recorded roughly 313 violations across the country, about two and a half times the previous year's total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 89 torture and ill-treatment violations (up from 51) and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540. A visitor in Kayseri faces this regime in the same way as anywhere else in Turkey, with the added exposure that any checkpoint or hospital interaction places identity documents and presentation in direct comparison.

On 29 October 2025 Human Rights Watch reported a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality for up to three years, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies for up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, on condition of permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warned it would force treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

Enforcement in Turkey has not waited for that draft to be enacted. Foreign visitors stopped at transit checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention, so every stop is an occasion on which a passport can be read against presentation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district, in shops and cafés, and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release; legal experts cited in that reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee reported that no fines were issued but she was documented anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as it was being applied to her.

Transition-related care is tightening in Kayseri specifically. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Kaos GL's 2025 review records 6 right-to-life violations, including 3 hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected, and notes that six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence that year. Violence of that kind reaches visitors through the same hostility a resident encounters: in August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker, who was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.
